title: How do you use broadcast join hints in Spark SQL (`SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(c) */ ... FROM transactions t JOIN customers c ON ...`)?
shortTitle: Broadcast join hints in Spark SQL

s1_definition.profdef: A broadcast join hint in Spark SQL is a comment-style directive placed immediately after the SELECT keyword that instructs the optimizer to broadcast a named table in the join, overriding the automatic size-based decision. The syntax is a hint block of the form `/*+ BROADCAST(table_alias) */`, naming the alias or table to broadcast. Spark also accepts the synonyms `BROADCASTJOIN` and `MAPJOIN`. The hint forces a Broadcast Hash Join on the named side regardless of the auto-broadcast threshold, provided the join type permits broadcasting that side.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the SQL hint is a sticky note on the work order that says "no matter what the size estimate says, photocopy the customers list for every clerk." Normally the records office decides automatically whether a list is small enough to copy, but the sticky note overrides that judgment for the named list. You put the note right at the top of the order, next to the word SELECT, and you name exactly which list to copy.
s1_definition.oneliner: Write `/*+ BROADCAST(alias) */` right after SELECT to force Spark to broadcast that table in the join, overriding the automatic threshold.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A broadcast join hint in Spark SQL is a comment-style directive placed immediately after the SELECT keyword that instructs the optimizer to broadcast a named table in the join, overriding the automatic size-based decision. The syntax is a hint block of the form `/*+ BROADCAST(table_alias) */`, naming the alias or table to broadcast. Spark also accepts the synonyms `BROADCASTJOIN` and `MAPJOIN`. The hint forces a Broadcast Hash Join on the named side regardless of the auto-broadcast threshold, provided the join type permits broadcasting that side.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the SQL hint is a sticky note on the work order that says "no matter what the size estimate says, photocopy the customers list for every clerk." Normally the records office decides automatically whether a list is small enough to copy, but the sticky note overrides that judgment for the named list. You put the note right at the top of the order, next to the word SELECT, and you name exactly which list to copy.

**One line to remember:** Write `/*+ BROADCAST(alias) */` right after SELECT to force Spark to broadcast that table in the join, overriding the automatic threshold.

sections.s2_technical:
The hint is written as a special comment block immediately following SELECT, using the markers that start with slash-star-plus and end with star-slash. Inside, you name the table or its alias, as in `/*+ BROADCAST(c) */` where c is the alias of the customers table. When Catalyst parses this, it marks that relation as a broadcast candidate and, during planning, chooses a Broadcast Hash Join that broadcasts the named side, bypassing the automatic size estimate and the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold. This is the SQL equivalent of wrapping a DataFrame in the broadcast function.

You can name more than one table in a single hint, as in `/*+ BROADCAST(c, d) */`, and Spark will consider broadcasting each. If you name both sides of a join, Spark broadcasts the smaller eligible one. Spark recognizes three equivalent keywords for this hint — BROADCAST, BROADCASTJOIN, and MAPJOIN — which all mean the same thing; the last comes from Hive heritage. There are also complementary join hints for other strategies, such as MERGE for sort-merge, SHUFFLE_HASH for shuffle hash join, and SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL for the nested loop join, so the hint system lets you steer the optimizer toward any strategy.

The hint is advisory with safety limits. If the named table is far too large to broadcast, Spark may ignore the hint rather than risk an out-of-memory failure, depending on the version, so a hint is not an absolute guarantee. For an outer join, you can only broadcast the side that is valid for that join type — for a left outer join you can broadcast the right side but not the left — and a hint on the wrong side is ignored. You use the hint for the same reasons as the DataFrame broadcast function: when statistics are stale or missing, when a table is small only after a filter the estimator cannot see, or when a size hovers just above the threshold and you do not want to change the global setting.

A senior-level nuance is placement and verification. The hint must appear right after the SELECT of the query block whose join you want to influence; a hint in the wrong query block or subquery may not apply. After adding the hint you confirm it took effect by running the query through explain and checking the physical plan for a BroadcastExchange and BroadcastHashJoin on the named side, because a silently ignored hint leaves a sort-merge join in place. With Adaptive Query Execution, a hint and AQE can interact, and the final executed plan in the Spark UI is authoritative.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a Spark SQL report joining the huge transactions table to a customers table. The customers table is small after filtering to a region, but Spark's estimate is above the threshold, so it plans a sort-merge join and the report is slow. This is exactly where the SQL broadcast hint helps — adding `/*+ BROADCAST(c) */` forces the broadcast.

Problem 2 — Another analyst writes the hint but places it in a subquery that is not the join block, so it has no effect. This shows the placement rule.

The demo parses a SQL string, detects whether a correctly placed broadcast hint names the intended table, and simulates the resulting join strategy, logging whether the hint applied and the resulting plan.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/spark-sql-hint-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.SqlHintDemo

# In a real Spark SQL job:
#   spark.sql("""
#     SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(c) */ t.txn_id, c.name

#     WHERE c.region = 'West'
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three SQL queries — one with a correctly placed BROADCAST hint on the customers alias, one using the MAPJOIN synonym, and one with no hint.

Step 1: For the first query, the interpreter finds the hint block right after SELECT, reads the keyword BROADCAST and the alias c, and confirms it matches the intended customers alias. It reports the hint applied and the join will be a broadcast hash join broadcasting customers.

Step 2: For the second query, it finds MAPJOIN, which is a synonym for BROADCAST, naming c. It reports the same outcome — the synonym has identical effect.

Step 3: For the third query, there is no hint, so the interpreter reports that the optimizer will decide by the threshold, which for a side above the threshold means a sort-merge join.

Step 4: The demo logs each interpretation and reminds the user to verify with explain that the broadcast exchange and broadcast hash join appear on the customers side.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:55:00 [INFO] Case 1: BROADCAST hint on 'c' APPLIED -> BroadcastHashJoin (broadcast c)
2026-10-30 04:55:00 [INFO] Case 2: MAPJOIN hint on 'c' APPLIED -> BroadcastHashJoin (broadcast c)
2026-10-30 04:55:00 [WARNING] Case 3: No top-level broadcast hint found -> optimizer decides by threshold (likely SortMergeJoin)
2026-10-30 04:55:00 [INFO] Verify with EXPLAIN that BroadcastExchange + BroadcastHashJoin appear on customers.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A broadcast join hint in Spark SQL is a comment-style directive you place immediately after the SELECT keyword to force the optimizer to broadcast a named table in a join, overriding the automatic size-based decision. The syntax is a hint block that starts with slash-star-plus and ends with star-slash, containing the keyword BROADCAST and the table alias, as in broadcast of the customers alias c. Spark also accepts the synonyms BROADCASTJOIN and MAPJOIN, which mean exactly the same thing, the last inherited from Hive. This is the SQL equivalent of wrapping a DataFrame in the broadcast function.

You can name more than one table in the hint, and Spark broadcasts the smaller eligible one; if you name both sides it picks the smaller. The hint belongs to a broader family of join hints — MERGE for sort-merge, SHUFFLE_HASH for shuffle hash, and SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL for nested loop — so you can steer the optimizer toward any strategy. I reach for the broadcast hint for the same reasons as the DataFrame broadcast function: stale or missing statistics, a table small only after a filter the estimator cannot see, or a size just above the threshold where I do not want to change the global setting.

At the National Bank of India our analysts used this constantly in Spark SQL reports. A join of the huge transactions table to a regionally filtered customers table was planned as a sort-merge because the estimate was above the threshold, and adding a broadcast hint on the customers alias flipped it to a fast broadcast join. The practical cautions I always give are that the hint must sit right after the SELECT of the join's own query block, not in an unrelated subquery, or it has no effect; that the hint is advisory, so Spark may ignore it if the table is far too large to broadcast safely; that for outer joins you can only broadcast the valid side; and that I always confirm with explain that a broadcast exchange and broadcast hash join actually appear on the named side, because a silently ignored hint leaves a sort-merge join in place.
